name: Essential amino acids (EAA)
summary: EAA supplements are mixtures of essential amino acids, the protein building blocks that must come from the diet. An EAA blend is not the same as a branched-chain amino acid (BCAA) product.
roles: Essential amino acids supply building blocks for proteins throughout the body.
BCAAs are leucine, isoleucine and valine: only part of the full essential amino acid group.

status.note: This basic guide does not provide a routine status test.

high.note: See the cautions below; this guide does not establish a safe upper amount.

examples: Soy, quinoa and combinations of pulses and grains
foodSources.note: Eating protein foods is not the same intervention as taking a free amino acid blend.

forms.name: Full EAA blend
forms.note: Contains the essential amino acids as free amino acids. The amount and balance of each ingredient vary by product.

forms.name: BCAA blend
forms.note: Contains only the branched-chain subset, not the full EAA group. BCAA and EAA are not interchangeable names.

reference.noUpperLimit: No tolerable upper intake level was found for essential amino acid blends as a whole. For the three branched-chain amino acids on their own, Germany's Federal Institute for Risk Assessment (BfR, 2019) derived guidance values for extra intake from supplements in adults: leucine 4.0 g, isoleucine 2.2 g, valine 2.0 g and 8.2 g in total a day. These do not cover children, pregnancy, breastfeeding, reduced kidney function or a low-protein diet.

sources.title: Food supplements: High intake of isolated branched-chain amino acids can lead to health impairments (BfR Opinion No. 052/2019)

interactions.note: Kidney disease can change how protein and amino acid intake is managed. Discuss an EAA product with your clinician rather than assuming it fits your nutrition plan.

cautions: Inherited amino acid disorders can make particular ingredients unsafe. A general EAA blend is not a substitute for a specialist formula for phenylketonuria or maple syrup urine disease.
EAA blends differ in their amino acid balance; safety information for one mixture does not establish a safe upper amount for every mixture.
Free amino acids do not provide all the nutrients in food and are not a complete meal replacement.

sources.title: Effect of Aerobic Exercise Training and Essential Amino Acid Supplementation for 24 Weeks on Physical Function, Body Composition, and Muscle Metabolism in Healthy, Independent Older Adults: A Randomized Clinical Trial.

origin: Essential amino acids are the nine amino acids the body cannot make: histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan and valine. They have to come from food.
EAA supplements are made from these in free form, as a powder. They are not the same as BCAA products, which contain only leucine, isoleucine and valine.
dosage: There is no reference intake and no upper limit for this ingredient. Studies use different blends, and a result for one mixture cannot be moved to another.
Check which amino acids and how much of each the label lists. People with inherited amino acid disorders or kidney disease should ask a clinician first.

foodAmounts.verdict: Yes, in principle. Protein foods such as meat, fish, eggs and dairy supply all nine essential amino acids, which is why animal foods are called complete proteins. This guide has no checked per-food figures for each amino acid, so it lists no amounts. See the protein powder guide for how much protein these foods give.
foodAmounts.notChecked: The food table used by this app does not measure individual amino acids.
